title: Framework Comparison
summary: React, Vue, and Svelte solve the same problem — turning state into UI — with genuinely different mental models, not just different syntax. This topic ties the whole group's concepts together into a fair, structured comparison for the 'you know React, explain X' interview question.

slides.markdown:
Every topic in this group has quietly been a framework comparison already — reactivity models, reconciliation, hooks — each covered React's approach alongside Vue's and Svelte's precisely because interviewers assume familiarity with more than one framework, even when the job only uses one.

This closing topic pulls those threads into a single, structured comparison, because the most common way this knowledge gets tested isn't "describe Svelte" in isolation — it's **"you know React, explain how Svelte's approach differs."** That phrasing rewards someone who can map unfamiliar concepts onto a mental model they already have, not someone reciting a second framework's docs from memory.

The goal here isn't to declare a winner. It's to be able to say, precisely, what's actually different (the reactivity model, the compile step) versus what's superficially different but structurally the same (JSX vs templates, both compiling to the same kind of update instructions).

slides.sectionTitle: Three mental models for the same problem
slides.markdown:
Every framework in this comparison answers "what changed, and how do I update the DOM for it" — the three differ in **when** they figure that out:

- **React**: re-render + virtual DOM. Doesn't track dependencies; re-runs the component function on state change and diffs the result against last time, at **runtime, on every update**.
- **Vue**: reactive refs, tracked via Proxies. Knows which values a piece of template depends on from the moment it's read, tracked at **runtime, once, during setup** — then reused on every subsequent update without re-discovering it.
- **Svelte**: compiled reactivity. The **compiler** analyzes your component source ahead of time and emits direct, targeted DOM-update instructions — there's no runtime dependency tracking or diffing machinery running in the browser at all; the analysis happened once, at build time.

Said as a spectrum: React discovers dependencies **every render**, Vue discovers them **once at runtime**, Svelte discovers them **once at compile time, before the app even runs**. Later work shifts earlier and earlier, which is the throughline for almost every other difference in this topic.

| | React | Vue 3 | Svelte |
|---|---|---|
| **What ships to the browser** | the framework runtime (React + ReactDOM) plus your component code | the framework runtime (smaller than React's) plus your component code | almost no framework runtime at all — the compiler outputs plain, targeted DOM-manipulation code per component |
| **Where the "framework work" happens** | in the browser, on every update (diffing) | in the browser, but pre-tracked (less repeated work than React) | mostly at build time; the browser just runs the generated update code |

The direct consequence: a small Svelte app can ship a meaningfully smaller bundle than the equivalent React app, because much of what React ships as a general-purpose runtime, Svelte's compiler bakes into component-specific code that only does exactly what that component needs — no generic diffing algorithm has to travel to the browser at all. This gap narrows as an app grows, though, since Svelte's compiled output scales with the number of components in a way a shared runtime doesn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Template syntax vs JSX vs compiled templates
slides.subTitle: Authoring experience
slides.markdown:
The most visible difference — and the least architecturally significant one — is what you actually type: - **React (JSX)**: markup written **inside** JavaScript — `
{user.name}
` is a function call in disguise, so you get the full power of JS (arbitrary expressions, `.map()` for lists) directly in markup, at the cost of needing a build step to transform JSX into `createElement` calls. - **Vue (templates)**: HTML-like syntax with special directives (`v-if`, `v-for`, `{{ }}` interpolation) — closer to plain HTML, which lowers the barrier for people coming from static markup, but expressions inside directives are a constrained subset of JS, not arbitrary code. - **Svelte (compiled templates)**: also HTML-like, but the compiler statically analyzes it to generate direct DOM operations — `{#each items as item}` compiles to exactly the loop needed for that specific list, not a generic templating engine interpreting the syntax at runtime. All three ultimately produce the same kind of output — instructions for building and updating a DOM tree — so this axis is genuinely a matter of authoring preference, not a functional trade-off, unlike the reactivity model.

slides.sectionTitle: Where each framework's reactivity work happens
slides.markdown: ![Spectrum bar showing when React, Vue, and Svelte perform dependency tracking](assets/dependency-tracking-spectrum.svg)

assets.alt: Spectrum bar showing when React, Vue, and Svelte perform dependency tracking

slides.markdown:
The concepts from earlier in this group — local state, lifting, Context-equivalents, external stores — exist in all three, under idiomatic names:

| Concept | React | Vue | Svelte |
|---|---|---|
| **Local state** | `useState` | `ref`/`reactive` | a plain `let` variable (reactivity is automatic via the compiler) |
| **Reach without drilling** | Context | `provide`/`inject` | context API (`setContext`/`getContext`), used less often since stores usually cover it |
| **Structured external store** | Redux, Zustand | Pinia | Svelte's built-in `writable`/`readable` stores — no separate library needed for the basic case |

Svelte's row is the most distinct: because reactivity is a compiler feature rather than a runtime API, even a "plain variable" (`let count = 0`) is reactive inside a Svelte component with no special wrapper call — a difference in authoring convenience that follows directly from the compile-time reactivity model, not an unrelated stylistic choice.

slides.sectionTitle: When the framework choice actually matters
slides.markdown:
Most framework debates on real teams are lower-stakes than they sound, because the concepts transfer almost completely — someone fluent in React's component model, state ownership rules, and reconciliation heuristics can become productive in Vue in days, not months, because they're learning new syntax for concepts they already understand deeply.

The choice matters more when it interacts with something structural:

- **Hiring pool and ecosystem size** — React's larger talent pool and library ecosystem is a real, practical factor for a growing team, independent of any technical merit.
- **Bundle-size-sensitive contexts** — a marketing site or an embedded widget where every kilobyte matters favors Svelte's near-zero runtime footprint.
- **Existing infra and team expertise** — a team with deep Vue investment (build tooling, internal libraries, institutional knowledge) rarely gets a good return from switching purely for a marginal technical edge elsewhere.

When none of those apply, it's frequently a preference call, and saying so explicitly — rather than overstating a technical case for one specific framework — reads as more credible than framework advocacy.

slides.sectionTitle: Treating syntax differences as architectural ones
slides.markdown:
A frequent mistake in comparison answers: pointing at JSX vs template syntax as if it were the *reason* one framework performs differently from another. Syntax is the most visible difference and the least consequential one — React, Vue, and Svelte all eventually produce the same kind of thing (DOM update instructions); the syntax is just how a developer expresses the intent, not how the framework decides what to update.

The differences that actually drive behavior are underneath the syntax: **when dependency tracking happens** (this topic's central spectrum) and **what runs in the browser versus at build time**. Two frameworks can look nearly identical in template syntax (Vue and Angular both use HTML-like templates, for instance) while having completely different reactivity models underneath, and two frameworks can look very different syntactically (JSX vs Svelte's HTML-like markup) while sharing more architecturally than people expect.

A candidate who says "Svelte doesn't use JSX" as the explanation for a performance difference has identified a real fact and drawn the wrong conclusion from it — the performance difference is the compile-time reactivity underneath, which happens to be paired with, but isn't caused by, the different-looking syntax.

A complete answer to this exact prompt, structured from what changed to what didn't:

1. **Name the reactivity model difference precisely.** "React re-runs the component function and diffs a virtual tree at runtime. Svelte's compiler statically analyzes the component ahead of time and emits direct DOM-update instructions — there's no virtual DOM, no runtime diffing, and often no component re-render at all."
2. **Connect it to an observable consequence.** "That's why Svelte apps tend to ship smaller bundles — much of what React ships as a general runtime, Svelte bakes into per-component compiled code instead."
3. **Note what's genuinely similar.** "Component composition, props-down-events-up, local vs shared state — all the same concepts, just different names: `let` instead of `useState`, `export let` instead of props."
4. **Avoid the syntax trap.** Don't attribute the performance difference to "no JSX" — the syntax is incidental; the compile-time dependency tracking is the actual mechanism.

This structure — mechanism, consequence, what transfers, what doesn't — is the same shape a strong answer takes for any "you know X, explain Y" framework question, not just this specific pairing, which is the actual skill this whole group has been building toward.
